name: 中華ソバ ビリケン (Chuka Soba Biliken)

claims.text: The shop's signature tare is a standard soy-sauce (shoyu) base built for a duck-and-chicken broth ramen; no wheat-free or tamari-based alternative was mentioned in any source, so the soy sauce used should be assumed to contain wheat as is typical for Japanese ramen tare.

name: フラックス カフェ (FLUX CAFE)

claims.text: お醤油にグルテンが入っているため『低グルテン』と表現 — the cafe describes itself as 'low gluten' because the soy sauce contains gluten; ramen/udon noodles are rice flour and fried chicken is potato starch, but seasoning is not gluten-free.
Concept is 低脂質・低グルテン・高タンパク (low-fat, LOW-gluten, high-protein) 'athlete meals' — the venue markets low-gluten, never gluten-free/celiac-safe.

'The dashi (broth) is made with bonito and kombu, with no granular dashi stock used' — confirms hidden katsuo/bonito (fish) in the base used across obanzai and soups, making dishes non-vegan by default.
Described as offering menus based on the concept 'グルテンフリーに近いおばんざい' (obanzai CLOSE TO gluten-free) — a deliberate hedge, not a gluten-free claim.
Third-party guide notes FLUX CAFE is NOT a dedicated gluten-free facility and serves regular gluten-containing items alongside low-gluten menu, implying cross-contamination risk for celiacs.
The soy sauce used in the kitchen contains a small amount of wheat/gluten; aside from that, wheat flour itself is largely avoided elsewhere in the kitchen.
Diners who are mindful of gluten can ask staff, who will suggest suitable menu items accordingly.
Noodles used for ramen/udon-style dishes and the dorayaki are made with rice flour, and the fried chicken is coated in potato starch instead of wheat flour, keeping most of the menu low in gluten.

name: ガシラ 渋谷店 (Gashira Shibuya-ten)

claims.text: No source confirms wheat-free (tamari) soy sauce is used or available; as a conventional izakaya it should be assumed standard wheat-containing shoyu is used throughout unless staff confirm otherwise.

name: 玄蕎麦しんがり 浅草本店 (Gensoba Shingari Asakusa Honten)

claims.text: The soba is 完全十割 (100% domestic whole buckwheat flour, no wheat binder), confirmed across multiple sources, but tempura using a wheat-flour batter is prepared in the same kitchen and no dedicated fryer or gluten-free handling protocol was confirmed.
Celiac reviewer notes that while the soba noodles are 100% buckwheat, the broth/tsuyu isn't gluten free; a customer who asked to have a meal made without soy sauce was told no.

Review content surfaced via aggregator listing: staff made sure not to include soya (often containing wheat) in the soup for one celiac guest — indicating accommodation is ad hoc and inconsistent, not a documented protocol.

Shop's own menu lists shrimp tempura, large-shrimp tempura, and kakiage (wheat-battered fried items) alongside 十割 soba, confirming an on-premises wheat fryer and cross-contamination exposure; no GF/allergen accommodation stated.
Menu items include 黒毛和牛すき玄蕎麦 (kuroge wagyu), 海老天 (shrimp tempura), 馬刺し (horse sashimi), 湯葉刺し (yuba) — an animal-protein-centric menu with conventional katsuo-dashi tsuyu, no vegan option found.
No source confirmed whether the tsuyu (dipping sauce) uses a wheat-free soy sauce; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and this has not been verified as gluten-free at this restaurant.

The menu is centered on animal proteins (wagyu beef, shrimp tempura, horse sashimi) and the tsuyu dipping sauce is very likely made with bonito (katsuo) dashi; no vegan-adapted dish or dashi substitution was found in available sources.

The base soba noodle is a genuine 100% buckwheat (juwari) product milled in-house from single-origin buckwheat and cut fresh per order, rather than a machine-made 2:8 blend that always contains wheat.

name: GLUTEN FREE CAFE avan 渋谷本店 (GLUTEN FREE CAFE avan Shibuya Honten)

claims.text: One English-language celiac reviewer reported becoming ill after eating the taco rice, cautioning that the shop's gluten-free claim may only mean wheat-flour-free rather than fully celiac-safe, and recommending caution for celiacs especially with savory menu items.

Another reviewer, noting it functions as a dedicated gluten-free facility, said staff seemed confident about what they could serve even with a language barrier, rating the experience positively (5 stars).

A reviewer reported becoming ill after having the taco rice and noted that, based on the shop's website, they seem to think 'gluten-free' only equals 'wheat free,' cautioning those with Celiac to be careful.
Tabelog listing title is now prefixed 【移転】/[Relocated] — 'GLUTEN FREE CAFE avan 渋谷本店' has relocated from the original Shinsen location.

Avan moved to JR Ueno station (Ecute Ueno) and now only serves churros (100% rice flour, takeout only); the menu changed significantly from when the negative taco rice review was posted, so the full savory menu (taco rice, fried chicken) described in the label no longer operates at this shop.
Staff are described across reviews as friendly and accommodating, going out of their way to meet customer requests, with both English and Japanese menus available.
Entire menu (not just desserts) is made without wheat flour, using rice flour milled from Yamagata Shonai-grown rice, which is the basis for its reputation as a dedicated gluten-free specialty shop.
The soba is made as a ni-hachi (2:8) blend, meaning wheat flour is mixed directly into the noodle dough as a binder — this is a structural gluten content issue, not just a cross-contamination risk.
The dashi/tsuyu for the signature dish is described as bonito-based with soy sauce, mirin, and sugar; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.
A vegan shojin soba is offered with a broth made from kombu and dried shiitake mushroom instead of bonito flakes, explicitly to accommodate diverse dietary needs.

name: 地鶏 海鮮 十割そば だししゃぶ 日日 新宿本店 (Jidori Kaisen Juwari Soba Dashi Shabu Nichin)

claims.text: The shop's own descriptions state the soba tsuyu is made with dashi from thick-cut Satsuma honkarebushi (薩摩本枯本節, dried bonito) roasted over binchotan — confirming bonito dashi in the tsuyu (non-vegan) and that the sauce is a kaeshi/soy-sauce base, which standard shoyu makes wheat-containing.
claims.source: https://gcft102.gorp.jp/ (via WebSearch summary of 日日 新宿本店 tsuyu description)

claims.text: General soba-tsuyu facts confirm 'soy sauce comprises a significant portion' of tsuyu and kaeshi is the soy-sauce base of restaurant tsuyu — i.e., the dipping sauce is inherently wheat-risk unless a special wheat-free shoyu is used, which is not advertised here.
Course examples for the Satsuma dashi-shabu explicitly include a tempura assortment (天ぷら盛り合わせ) finished with itasoba — wheat batter and shared-fryer cross-contamination in the same kitchen.
No result for 日日/Nichinichi soba appears on FindMeGlutenFree or HappyCow celiac listings for Shinjuku/Tokyo — no independent celiac-grade evidence of any gluten-free handling exists.
claims.source: https://www.findmeglutenfree.com/jp/shinjuku-city/dinner (search returned no listing for this shop)

claims.text: The restaurant is a jidori/kaisen izakaya (chicken, seafood, sake) with dashi-shabu as its signature; searches for グルテンフリー/アレルギー返し return no allergen accommodation or GF protocol for this location.

The signature soba is juwari (十割そば) — 100% buckwheat made with stone-ground flour and no wheat flour binder — which is a naturally wheat-free noodle base, unlike standard soba blended with wheat flour.

name: ジカセイ メンショウ (Jikasei MENSHO (Shibuya PARCO))

claims.text: Noodles use a wheat-based dough with quinoa mixed in only to reduce gluten content, not eliminate it; the shop shares a kitchen that also makes wheat-containing soy-sauce ramen.
Vegan dandan and vegan miso ramen are prepared in the same kitchen as the restaurant's chicken-paitan and A5-wagyu ramen.
Cross-contamination in the cooking environment cannot be guaranteed; guests with severe allergies are advised to confirm directly with the shop before ordering.
English-language reviewers praise friendly, accommodating staff and a clearly marked vegan menu, calling it a convenient, warming stop near Shibuya Crossing.
Ordering screens include English options, easing the process for non-Japanese-speaking vegan diners.
